Even by President Trump’s standards, this is a bit of a bombshell.

   Wednesday evening, shortly after Trump’s new Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh led the board toward a unanimous vote to increase interest rates , the president revealed that they had discussed this very decision beforehand.

   “I talked to Kevin,” Trump told reporters. “I said ‘you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter.’ The board is very hostile. They are very political. They are doing the wrong thing. They are a bunch of politicians.”

   During a press conference before Trump’s comments, Warsh asserted the Fed’s independence. The Fed said it raised interest rates to combat inflation, which remains stubbornly high.

   There is little modern precedent for a Fed chairman consulting with the president about a decision to raise interest rates. Trump’s comments made it sound like Warsh almost asked for Trump’s permission. The Fed—so far—has refused to clarify what exactly they talked about. Or, just as importantly, when the conversation took place. Did they talk Wednesday morning? Last week? How long has Trump known this? Did Warsh disclose to other members of the Fed that he had consulted with Trump?

   Trump famously berated Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for not doing more to cut interest rates. And so Warsh’s move to raise rates might have sent Trump into a tizzy. So maybe Warsh was trying to foam the runway, in a sense. But Warsh’s term as Fed chairman runs past Trump’s term. So would he consult with Trump’s successor like this? What if it’s a Democrat?

   A little story.

   More than 20 years ago, when I was a reporter at the American Banker newspaper, I filed a Freedom of Information Act request seeking the calendar and phone logs of then-Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan. The materials were produced the week after he left office (suspicious timing? Ya think?). The most interesting thing in the phone logs was this: Greenspan regularly consulted with a young Bush administration White House staffer about housing-finance giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. This received a lot of attention because calls between the White House and “independent” Fed chair were supposed to be few and far between. That young White House staffer? Kevin Warsh.

Senior administration officials have gathered almost daily in recent months to discuss AI risks and push for guardrails even as Trump dismisses calls for tighter federal regulation. Or, just as importantly, when the conversation took place. Did they talk Wednesday morning? Last week? How long has Trump known this?
